title: Why the limit

blocks.md:
## Too much current

Current is not a score you maximize. If current goes past the cap, wires and the lamp heat up. Brightness is one goal; **safe current** is the other. In this one-cell loop, current is about `1 / ohms`. The cap we gave you is **2**, so ohms of `1` gives current `1` (bright enough and under the cap) while ohms of `0.25` gives current `4`.

This bites when you chase the brightest looking setting and pick `0.25` or `0`. The lamp may look great in a sloppy model, then the constraint fails. Heat is the real-world version of that failure. A brighter bulb that melts its own wire is not a brighter circuit you get to keep.

```text
battery → resistor(1 Ω) → lamp → battery
current ≈ 1 / 1 = 1    (under the cap of 2)
```

A common mistake is setting resistance to `0` so current is huge, or to `0.25` so current is `4`. The question asks which move is safer when you want a brighter lamp in this one-cell loop. Pick the resistance that raises brightness without crossing `2`.

blocks.promptMd: You want a brighter lamp. Which move is safer in this one-cell loop?

choices.md: Set resistance to 0 so current is huge
Set resistance to 1 (current 1, brighter, under the cap)

blocks.explainMd: Brightness rose at ohms=1 without crossing 2. 0.25 looks brighter in a sloppy model but fails the constraint.

description: Learn why too much current is a problem, and what a safe limit is for.
